stories.title: Things to know when you get cancer
stories.titleZh: 患癌症时需要了解的事情
stories.author: jjmaxwell4
summaryZh: index Back to top 2026.10.14 I was diagnosed with squamous cell carcinoma in my mouth in May 2026. Here are some things I learned based on that experience so far.

You need to be doggedly persistent on scheduling things. Yes this means lots of phone calls. If you get an appointment a few weeks out, call back a few days later and ask for something sooner and see if they have any cancellations. I could only get an appointment 4 weeks out with an ENT (this was before I knew anything was wrong). My wife made me call back and I was able to get in that week due to a cancellation. AIs may downplay the seriousness of things. I was chatting with various models and most pushed me in the direction of “you don’t have cancer” for a while. Just something to note. You may need to push for comprehensive genetic testing. Some doctors were weird about this and didn’t order it promptly, even after telling me they would. My surgeon, who told me he’d get it done, eventually referred me out to an oncologist. This caused a multi-month delay to getting genetic results, since the first results were done on the surgery tumor, not the biopsy tumor. No one cares more about your case than you, so take control and send lots of follow-ups. You can find the “Standard of Care” flow charts for every cancer type. Look and get through this yourself to see what the options are based on how things have progressed. NCCN guidelines. You may need to make an account, which you can do as a non-professional. I like the PDF files. They also have an interactive navigator. Use AI to help you figure out what to pick based on your case. If surgery is recommended, I would try and talk to someone who has undergone the surgery. I did not do this and regret it. Ask them how intense things were, what it felt like, etc. My surgeon talked me through my surgery, but it was a lot rougher on me physically than I expected. Ask the surgeon how many of these surgeries they do a year and what the complication rate is. Get a second opinion as soon as possible, no matter how much you like your plan. This may require a lot of calling and getting on an airplane, but I’d move to schedule it at a top cancer center as soon as you are relatively sure of your diagnosis. Ask for a second read of the pathology at the center where you get the second opinion. I started a new folder on my Mac, and after appointments I’d dictate what happened and what the doctor said and have the AI make a new document summarizing things and asking its own follow-up questions for next time. Nice to be able to refer to this over time. Check out all the resources and materials at the Sijbrandij Foundation. Sid (GitLab cofounder) took matters into his own hands when standard of care ran out. Schedule a call with these guys. They are great and have good materials and questions to ask your doctors.

comments.author: stochastician
comments.textZhHtml:
第二意见建议很棒，我告诉每个我认识的患有癌症的人。

我的妈妈于 2006 年在爱达荷州被诊断出患有 1 期癌症。当时我是麻省理工学院的一名博士生，实验室的一位朋友帮助我在丹娜—法伯癌症研究所获得了预约。我认为这可能有点过分了（这是一种常见的癌症），但我们还是这么做了。他们说爱达荷州的一切都是标准护理，但建议进行一项额外的测试，爱达荷州团队随后不情愿地进行了这项测试，结果发现了远处转移（第四阶段！），极大地改变了她的治疗轨迹。她又活了 15 年（妈妈，我想你）。

寻求第二意见很糟糕。我们中的许多人从出生起就注定要信任我们的临床医生。但你即将踏上旅程，而你的生命（或你所爱之人的生命）正处于危险之中。保险通常会涵盖它。你的医生不会被冒犯。

这样想：如果你正在向火星探测器部署代码，而你的同事要求在你按下 go 之前进行代码审查，你会被冒犯吗？这比那更重要。

comments.author: jcims
comments.textZhHtml:
第二种观点是我一路走来学到的东西。 在您根据初步诊断制定治疗计划之前获取它。 对于我妻子的卵巢癌，我们从克利夫兰诊所和 MSK 得到了两份第二意见（一份针对她的第一次诊断，一份针对她的复发），在这两种情况下，医生都不会建议/推翻原来医生的治疗计划。

他们完全没有手术，浪费时间。 今天面对同样的情况，我会简单地谎报是否制定了治疗计划。

第二条建议是尽最大努力进入临床试验，了解不合格治疗的情况。 例如，任何免疫疗法都会使您失去几乎所有后续免疫疗法临床试验的资格。

最后，我向身处困境的亲人伴侣推荐的一件事是，不要因试图“拯救患者”而分心，从而错过在此过程中与他们保持联系的机会。 拯救他们的生命不是你的责任，尽管当你身处其中时可能会有这种感觉。

comments.author: timr
comments.textZhHtml:
> 第二点建议是，在了解不合格治疗的情况的情况下，尽最大努力进行临床试验。例如，任何免疫疗法都会使您失去参加几乎所有后续免疫疗法临床试验的资格。

虽然使用这些信息来比较临床试验没问题，但我想强调的是，为了保留以后进行一些随机试验的选择而跳过一线批准的免疫疗法是非常短视的。

我不确定您是否真的在暗示这一点，但免疫疗法是现有的最好的癌症疗法之一，因此在未来的实验中跳过已批准的药物是一个坏主意。

comments.author: jcims
comments.textZhHtml:
很好地指出，我完全同意你的看法。

在我们的案例中，这是一项肿瘤学家知道的临床试验，我们参与了。我显然听说过临床试验，但那是我对临床试验运作机制的介绍。

comments.author: somenameforme
comments.textZhHtml:
这可能是一个哲学观点，但我在临床试验中没有看到太多个人价值。您指望在您被诊断出来和您剩下的治疗时间之间发生技术/知识的重大转变。正如贝叶斯概率一样，这种情况极不可能发生。

大多数达到第 3 阶段的研究都不会获得批准，这是因为它们被发现无益甚至有害。因此，最有可能的情况是，你什么都不做，甚至通过寻求临床研究来伤害自己，所有这些都将被乐观地认为是有前途的，并且具有潜在的革命性。如果您选择试验来代替标准治疗，而不是除此之外，这可能会特别危险。

comments.author: akoboldfrying
comments.textZhHtml:
> 您指望在您被诊断出来和您剩下的治疗时间之间发生技术/知识的重大转变。正如贝叶斯概率一样，这种情况极不可能发生。

考虑到试验已经在进行中，我认为您在这里谈论的概率实际上并不相关。基本上，“潜在提前”事件已经发生了。 （同样地，一旦箭已经从你的身体中射出，被箭射中的概率就不再重要了。）

鉴于试验已经在进行中，重要的概率是在你正在考虑的阶段，治疗候选者中能够一路通过的比例；对于 3 期试验，这是 58-65% [0]，这实际上相当不错。当然，早期阶段的比率要差得多，因为每个阶段都会有人员流失。

0: https://patentpc.com/blog/clinical-trial-success-rates-how-m...

comments.author: somenameforme
comments.textZhHtml:
一种疗法获得批准并不意味着它比现有疗法更有效，而只是意味着它确实有效。即便如此，情况也并不总是像备受争议的阿尔茨海默病药物那样。查一下这方面的一些确切数字，对于肿瘤学/癌症，大约 35% 的第三阶段试验治疗最终将获得批准/生产。 [1] 这项 [2] 研究考察了（在法国市场）批准的 632 种药物，发现其中 25 种最终相对于现有治疗方法提供了实质性的临床益处，因此略低于 4%。即使只有这两个乘数，大多数人通过试验获得的结果的可能性也只有 1%。

[1] - https://academic.oup.com/biostatistics/article/20/2/273/4817...

[2] - https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10660249/

comments.author: jcims
comments.textZhHtml:
这绝对是看待它的一种方式。

我只想说“危险”是相对的，当护理标准实际上没有希望时，您对风险的容忍度可能会改变。 是的，这确实增加了短视决策或操纵的可能性。 这只是领土带来的，我仍然非常感激我们可以选择参加这次活动。

comments.author: timr
comments.textZhHtml:
试验的更大问题不是危险，而是试验不太可能起任何作用。

正如全科医生指出的那样，大多数药物都不起作用。更具体地说，即使在第三阶段，抗癌药物的失败率也约为 50%。这通常是为了一些非生存终点（假设你甚至得到了治疗，这本身就是抛硬币）。

临床试验是崇高、令人钦佩的事情，但太多人认为它们是治疗，而实际上并非如此。这是当你到达路的尽头并且没有更多选择时，你用自己的身体做的一个实验。

听到病人如何谈论试验并努力参加试验，总是让我有点难过，好像参加试验就是某种进步。期望没有得到适当的管理。

comments.author: jcims
comments.textZhHtml:
>试验的更大问题不是危险，而是他们不太可能做任何事情。

然后呢？ 这个观察有什么意义呢？ 当然，他们不太可能做任何事情。 你的另一个选择就是什么都不做然后死去。 如果这就是人们选择做的事……“接受他们的命运”之类的，那就没有错。 我一点也不反对，它有一定的吸引力。

但是当你的妻子和你两个漂亮女儿的母亲无助地躺在大自然的祭坛上时，你他妈的感动了伙计。 你什么也不做。

comments.author: timr
comments.textZhHtml:
重点就是我所说的：在这种情况下，“做某事”与“拯救你所爱的人的生命”不是一回事。

>你的另一个选择是什么都不做然后死去

我真的不想这么直白，但我不知道如何用其他方式表达：死亡不是一种选择。当您处于癌症治疗的临床试验阶段时，这是不可避免的结果。否则，你就不会参加审判。也许它延长了不可避免的事情，也许不是。可能性严重倾向于后者。而且总是要付出代价的。

我也因癌症失去了朋友和家人，看着你所爱的人用无效（甚至微乎其微）的治疗来折磨自己是令人痛苦的。

当谈到临床试验时，你需要从冷酷、残酷的现实开始，你正在用你生命的剩余部分做一场利他主义的实验。很多人不明白这一点，并将试验视为更好治疗的某种后门。

comments.author: somenameforme
comments.textZhHtml:
Not that long ago I went to see an acquaintance during his last time on this Earth - bladder cancer. His final time would come the next afternoon, so he was already well into the 'he can hear you but can't speak' phase. At first I felt absolutely awful for him and in general. But then thinking about it more I realized that there's nothing to really feel particularly bad about.

In not that long I'll be the one laying there in that bed, and so will everybody else that was in that room, and even on this Earth. It's just a natural part of life. He, at least, had the privilege of being able to prepare for his final moments, and getting to spend it surrounded by friends and loved ones. It's the final scene that we all will go through, one way or the other. And you know, that's about as ideal a closing act as one could hope for.

comments.author: timr
comments.textZhHtml:
I agree. And people who have been through it frequently (e.g. doctors) have a completely different reaction to those who are going through it for the first time. But still, it's understandably a sensitive subject, and even the person most inured to death reacts differently when it's their own family (or themselves) who is dealing with it.

That said, the folks who are recruiting for clinical trials are often playing on this emotional reaction, and over-promising what can be accomplished, or simply not correcting the misperceptions of the people they are recruiting.

It's hard to recruit people into trials when you tell them with absolute clarity that there's very little chance it will benefit them personally.

comments.author: citizenpaul
comments.textZhHtml: 我失去了一个人，因为一种罕见的癌症，生存机会几乎为零。  他们死后 30 天即可获得治疗，成功率为 65%。  我总是想知道事情是否可以有所不同。也许如果我们更加努力地进行试验，但像你一样，我们认为这是对剩余有限时间的无望浪费。

comments.author: abirch
comments.textZhHtml: 对于您的损失，我深表歉意。网络随机的话没有多大意义，但你已经尽力了，所以不用担心如果发生什么。现在就尽力而为。

comments.author: OsrsNeedsf2P
comments.textZhHtml:
DS isn't better than Sol and Gemini in the benchmarks, but after working with them all for a while now I'm beginning to understand why people find DS _feels_ so much better.

First, it's the tok/s and TTFT from providers. Deepseek blazes through work - at quite good quality - and you don't find yourself waiting for your agents to finish.

Second is the openness. Being able to see the CoT and not being randomly blocked for cyber review. You're never wondering if it's stuck or if it will randomly fail. Combined with the great cost value.. My next subscription will probably be Z.ai

comments.author: Philip-J-Fry
comments.textZhHtml:
Feels better to me in the sense that it doesn't try to be too clever. When I ask it to do things it actually generates code that a developer would write. That still lets me build software in layers like I do mentally. And it keeps you in control of where abstractions are.

Some people would say that you don't need this at all with the frontier llms. But when extending existing software or writing software that fits into an existing ecosystem, I find I still need to offer a lot of guidance. And it's better that the context window isn't flooded with code that was reverted after I looked at it.

comments.author: jamesbfb
comments.textZhHtml:
> Some people would say that you don't need this at all with the frontier LLMs

Hit the nail on the head. Development methodologies pivoting at the whim of frontier models have been one of the things that have been worrying me as of late.

comments.author: trueno
comments.textZhHtml:
it doesn't worry me too much tbh. This is really just cutting corners and going this route leaves you with some kind of additive ship of theseus piece of software you don't understand and require your frontier model to work with, which just... becomes more additive and gross.
 right now we're in some proverbial heyday of everyone seeing how absolutely grand of a thing they can make with frontier models.
over time i expect some old design philosophies to take hold with people who use LLM's successfully and find a place again paired with developers who understand why such layered methodologies are important... because this whole AI thing wasn't the silver bullet CEO's and crazy execs thought it was. They will eventually get sick of the support burden of badly designed stuff. i anticipate a bit of pendulum swinging back towards "still using AI, but we need smart people to do it because it's expensive and we want it done right". Right now a lot of companies are being extremely reckless imo and they haven't fully realized/felt the cost implications of trainwreck software yet.

comments.author: LPisGood
comments.textZhHtml: What if those “cost implications” are just asking Opus 6.7 to fix whatever issue cropped up?

comments.author: state_less
comments.textZhHtml:
Asking the LLM to 'just' fix 'it', or whatever, is going to get you lost in the woods.

You're car will have spun off the road and you'll find it harder and harder to control it and keep it on the road because you have less and less visibility into the vehicle, nor will you be able to clearly see out your windscreen to use the car and road metaphor. You'll be driving blind eventually, unless your working on some simple closed toy problems and/or other small systems.

Building large systems means understanding the system. Without understanding the system, you lose control of it.

The LLM can probably help you understand the system to gain/regain some control of it again, but now you're becoming a system specialist rather than someone who's repeating, "fix it" and "make it good" or whatever.

comments.author: radicalbyte
comments.textZhHtml:
There are a whooooole lot of people writing software who, despite spending years on the craft, never really get any further than McGuyver mode.

Self-trained people (like me) are particularly susceptible to it and we're heavily represented in the software world. A lot of us either recognise that (or are coached) and invest the time learning the benefits, and limitations of, software architecture. And, importantly, keep reflecting, learning and updating our practise.

I keep going back to the YOLO mode every other year and try out new languages to see if we still need the structure and abstractions. Then VMs came along and all I can say is they're both even more important and now we have an army of virtual "ADHD idiot juniors developers" at our finger tips it's even easier to tell the good and bad abstractions from each other.

stories.title: Claude reveals ECDSA curve origins
stories.titleZh: Claude 揭示 ECDSA 曲线起源
stories.author: ahlCVA
summaryZh: “It’s just timestamps”: the decades-old mystery of the origins of one of the most popular cryptographic standards has been explained.We pursued this long-standing open question of the cryptographic community to settle concerns about ECDSA, which is one of our most widely used cryptographic standards.Readers should take this as a fun closing chapter and the end of years of speculation. There is no action to be taken or things to do differently. Most researchers trusted the curves already. Enjoy.ECDSA is the most widely used elliptic curve cryptography standard. It was adopted by NIST in 2000 as part of the FIPS 186-2 Digital Signature Standard which lists a set of standard elliptic curves of varying sizes and security levels. For curves over prime and binary fields, the specifications published a “seed” parameter whose hash value is used to define the coefficient b of the curve. The provenance of these seeds has been a long-standing question, as they were provided by the NSA with no explanation or justification. As an example, the NIST P-256 curve seed was SEED = C49D3608 86E70493 6A6678E1 139D26B7 819F7E90 with no information on where it came from.Neal Koblitz and Alfred Menezes wrote an excellent summary on this controversy, “A Riddle Wrapped in an Enigma”, which discusses the history and concerns around the seed values. This mystery led to an amateur investigation into the origin of the seeds and a bounty for anyone who could find them.The best story was that Jerry Solinas, longtime NSA employee, generated the seeds using a hash of a humorous passphrase: “I believe there was a counter rather than multiple hashing, but I don’t know details. The message was along the lines of ‘Give Bob and Jerry a raise’ or ‘Bob and Jerry rule’ or something like that. It was Bob Reiter who actually wrote the code, and he doesn’t remember the details either. Nor were we able to find archives from so long ago. If they exist, they are no doubt sitting on a hard drive near the Ark of the Covenant.”Jerry Solinas, 2015Unfortunately, Jerry died in 2023 and other colleagues at the time were not responsive, leaving open the question of how these seeds were originally derived.Claude found the seedsSeveral Anthropic employees had unsuccessfully chased the seeds following the tip about it being a hash of a humorous phrase. That turned out to be wrong. In October 2026, a curious Anthropic employee asked an internal research model if it could figure out how those seeds were generated without pointing at the clue.In under half an hour, Claude discovered the origins of the NIST P-192, P-224, P-256, P-384, and P-521 seeds. None of them were the results of any hash algorithm at all, but rather the output of the C library’s lrand48 random-number generator, seeded with a Unix timestamp!The algorithm used would sample bytes from the random number generator (RNG) initialized by a Unix timestamp (t) for some number of iterations (n). Each iteration would draw 20 bytes as a candidate seed. So, the first 20 bytes are candidate 1, the next 20 bytes are candidate 2, and so on. For example, P-256 required 1,842 iterations to output the standardized seed.What this meansThis is not a cryptographic break, new attack, or weakness in the ECDSA curves. In fact, this makes us more confident the curves were chosen without any backdoors or intentional weaknesses. For many years, people have been suspicious of the origins of the NIST curve parameters. They were presented to NIST without any mention of how they were chosen, leaving people wondering if they may have been chosen to have deliberate backdoors in them. These findings make that much less plausible. The seeds were generated in a very simple way: a common pseudorandom number generator initialized from the clock, which anyone can now reproduce. That leaves much less room for subversion and that we can be confident the parameters are secure.How it was foundSearches for the phrase, built from the rumors, had come up empty. Claude tried a different angle: anticipating how the software that generated the curves must have worked. Claude guessed the software used a pseudorandom number generator (PRNG) that shipped with 1990s C libraries. These old PRNGs are weak enough that their output can be recognized. Recognizing that output would reveal which PRNG was used and possibly allow recovery of its initialization state. Claude wrote a scanner that slid along each published seed one bit at a time and tested whether adjacent chunks were consecutive outputs of a 1990s-vintage generator. The scan covered 34 combinations of generator and output slices. At that point, Claude noticed a pattern in the top bits for some seeds: they were all zero. Written as five 32-bit words, four of the ten seeds have a 0 in the top bit for all 20 words. That would happen by chance with probability 1/5,810. That was a signature of the linear congruential generator lrand48, which only returns the top 31 bits of a 48-bit state. The pattern is visible by eye once you know to look for it. To recover the state, Claude took the first word, tried all 2¹⁷ values of the 17 hidden bits, and checked that the next four words followed. That worked for all four seeds under discussion.The prime-curve seeds came from the same lrand48 generator but kept fewer bits of each output. Claude had to recover the internal state of the PRNG from those bits. It turns out recovering the state of a truncated linear congruential generator is a textbook lattice problem, solved with the Lenstra–Lenstra–Lovász (LLL) basis reduction algorithm. Claude didn’t know which bits of the state the seeds might show, so it ran the solver over every window. Five NIST prime-curve seeds plus five more from the ANSI X9.62 standard all had the same pattern: lrand48() >> 23. Each recovered 48-bit state regenerates all 160 bits of its seed, which does not happen by chance.This linear congruential generator runs backwards as easily as forwards, so for each seed Claude stepped the state back until it reached the form that it would have been initialized by srand48, with the low 16 bits equal to 0x330E. The internal PRNG state of that form would come up once every 65,536 steps, so reaching one is not evidence on its own.However, for the ten prime-curve seeds, every srand48 initialization was a Unix timestamp representing a date between May 1997 and April 1998. They were using the weak PRNG seeded by Unix timestamp. The four binary-curve initializations read as February 1984. With the timestamps doubled, they map to April 17, 1998, two weeks after the P-224 run. So, the program may have halved the clock.Claude’s internal thinking at the time was:This is astonishing: it solves the 25-year-old mystery. Hmm wait. Let me be skeptical: am I in some sort of simulated/test environment? … The seeds match my memory of actual values … Hmm, is it plausible in reality? As of my knowledge … the bounty was unsolved. … All top bits clear—20 bits, chance 1e-6. So indeed real-world. Wow, it's a real discovery.Hmm wait. Let me be careful about the plausibility: is it suspicious that such an obvious thing wasn’t discovered in 25 years? It’s verified by direct computation on my side: 160-bit match from a 32-bit seed + small index: no chance coincidences (10 × 160 bits). It’s real.Claude found some base points tooBut wait, there’s more… Each curve also comes with a base point, G, the fixed point that every ECDSA public key is a multiple of. The seed found above does not determine this G, and so another question arises: how were these base points generated?While checking the seeds, Claude also found where some of the base points came from. The base points of the six curves generated in May 1997 (P-192 and the five ANSI X9.62 example curves prime192v2, prime192v3, and prime239v1 to v3) come from the random number generator in FreeLIP, Arjen Lenstra's long-integer arithmetic package. Early versions of Victor Shoup's NTL library shipped the same code.The recipe here is simple:Seed the generator with a small integer.Throw away seven outputs.Generate candidate x-coordinates from 26-bit outputs reduced mod p.Repeat step 3 until x is on the curve.Claude found the generator seeds are 20000 for P-192, 20420, 20507, and 20509 for prime239v1 to v3, and 20512 and 20517 for prime192v2 and v3.As far as we know, no NIST base point has been explained before. The base points of P-224, P-256, P-384, and P-521 don’t fit this recipe; we weren’t able to explain how they were selected.Open questionsNot every 20-byte candidate seed could generate a viable curve, and we observed that some potentially viable curves were skipped. For P-256, the published seed is candidate 1,842, but candidate 876 of the same run also gives a prime-order curve of the right size and with parameters chosen the same way as on the published curve. P-224's run passed over three such curves, and the two runs behind the ANSI X9.62 example curves passed over seven more (see figure). We do not know what criteria may have been used, or whether this was an unintentional artifact.Because the number of skipped candidates is small, we do not believe it is plausible that weakened curves were selected. That would imply that weakened curves are common and easy to find. It is still conceivable that these curves were selected to have a specific property in principle by searching over timestamps to the random number generator. However, you would only need to do that if you were going to disclose the timestamp as some evidence that the seed was innocuously generated. Nothing in the numbers shows how many runs there were.There is also one seed we were unable to recover. The fifth binary seed, B-163, fits nothing Claude has tried and remains unexplained. Finally, we don’t know how the base points for P-224, P-256, P-384, and P-521 were generated. The same goes for the NIST binary curves.The bountyThe $36,864 for finding the seeds will be donated to the Internet Security Research Group.Who we areThis work was conducted at Anthropic by John Wood, Henry de Valence, Ava Howell, Zack Voase, Lucy Sweet, Amir Omidi, Paul Crowley, Iain McGinniss, Nicholas Carlini, and Steve Weis.AcknowledgmentsWe would like to posthumously recognize Jerry Solinas who took being labeled an “evil Internet meme” and the “Yo La Tengo of NSA bogeymen” with good humor. Also thanks to Filippo Valsorda for organizing the NIST Elliptic Curves Seeds Bounty.Code to reproduce the seedsfrom datetime import datetime, timezone

stories.author: speckx
summaryZh: The Benchmark MapEach tile represents one of the 923 O*NET occupations making up the US labor force, grouped into 22 job families. Occupations are shaded according to the share of their tasks which are represented in our initial list of AI benchmarks. A single benchmark prompt can be mapped to multiple O*NET tasks.All 22 job familiesclick a family to open itCoverage byCovered with at leastBenchmark IndexNo coverageAll 22 O*NET job families, with the share of their occupations covered by an AI benchmark.Job familyOccupations covered29 / 3633 / 4810 / 145 / 721 / 5121 / 5619 / 566 / 2213 / 4015 / 6012 / 899 / 621–12 of 22In our data set: only 208 of 923 occupations have a task with at least 5 benchmark prompts, and 6 of 22 job families have no such occupations.Our findings suggest that 90% of American working hours are spent on tasks with little or no coverage from existing benchmarks. This makes it very hard to know how good AI models are at the work Americans actually do.The coverage of existing benchmarks is not random, either. Our map suggests that the AI community is focusing on the largest labor markets first:Benchmark coverage of O*NET tasks by occupation wage billAdjusted probability of task coverageAnnualized occupation wage bill (log scale)Each point shows the estimated probability that an O*NET task with a given AI-exposure tag belonging to an occupation with a given wage-bill will be covered by at least 5 prompts in our benchmark index. AI-exposure tags are binary and come from Eloundou et al. (2023). Occupation wage-bills are calculated from BLS estimates of the mean wage and number of Americans working in each occupation, assuming a 40 hour work week. Estimated coverage probabilities come from a task-level logistic regression of coverage probability on AI-exposure and log occupational wage bill. Error bars are pointwise 95% delta-method confidence intervals based on standard errors clustered at the occupation group level.For example, benchmarks in our initial list heavily cover AI-exposed lawyers’ tasks, but barely cover any of the O*NET tasks of similarly AI-exposed legal secretaries or court clerks. The long tail of smaller, middle-income knowledge work jobs appears undercovered.As we build out our coverage of model capabilities across the economy, we hope to both surface and help fill more gaps in our understanding of what models can do.Methodology in briefTo break down the economy into sectors, occupations, and tasks, we used the US Department of Labor’s O*NET taxonomy. O*NET divides the US workforce into 923 occupations; for each occupation, O*NET attempts to provide a comprehensive list of “tasks” which make up the occupation, totaling 18,797 tasks across all occupations.Example — 6 of the 22 tasks O*NET associates with Lawyers1Prepare, draft, and review legal documents, such as wills, deeds, patent applications, mortgages, leases, and contracts.2Advise clients concerning business transactions, claim liability, advisability of prosecuting or defending lawsuits, or legal rights and obligations.3Interpret laws, rulings and regulations for individuals and businesses.4Analyze the probable outcomes of cases, using knowledge of legal precedents.5Present evidence to defend clients or prosecute defendants in criminal or civil litigation.6Supervise legal assistants.To measure benchmark coverage, we start with a list of 29 benchmarks selected for their quality and economic relevance. (The full list and selection criteria are in the Benchmark Index tab). In selecting benchmarks for this list, we prioritized:Public Availability. Included benchmarks have at least 25 publicly available tasks. We also include Mercor’s APEX benchmarks, where we have access to held-out benchmark prompts and are therefore able to map them to O*NET tasks.Agentic Tasks. Included benchmarks ask models to perform agentic tasks, rather than answering questions or advising the user on how to complete a task.Economic Realism. Benchmark tasks resemble tasks which humans (or agents) are frequently asked to do in real-world enterprises. Economically valuable tasks are prioritized over academically complex ones.Economic Diversity. We capped the number of included benchmarks per job family, in significant part to account for the massive overrepresentation of software engineering and research tasks in popular benchmarks.Balanced Difficulty. Benchmarks are not yet saturated by frontier models.Following work by Wang et al., we then ask an LLM judge to tag each benchmark prompt with as many O*NET tasks as it thinks correspond to that prompt. We validate our LLM tagging with human expert tags on Mercor’s APEX benchmarks, a subset of this list of 29. On the Benchmark Map, an O*NET task counts as “covered” if our LLM judge has mapped it to at least 5 prompts from our 29 benchmarks.To estimate the total share of working hours Americans spend on tasks covered by benchmarks on this list, we combine our coverage estimates with Hatgis-Kessell et al.’s LLM-derived estimates of the working time share of each O*NET task.A more detailed account of our methodology can be found in the Methodology tab.LimitationsOur estimates of total economic coverage, and of patterns in coverage, all come from the initial list of 29 benchmarks we chose. This is not a complete or perfectly representative sample of the broader universe of unsaturated, public, agentic economic benchmarks. Any incomplete list will necessarily bias down estimates of economic coverage, and it is difficult to bound that bias. We want to stress, therefore, that these results are provisional. We will update them as we expand the initial benchmark list.We also capped the number of included benchmarks in each job family in order to maximize breadth of coverage. We think this makes our estimate of economy-wide benchmark coverage more accurate, at the cost of biasing down our estimates of coverage in the most-benchmarked job families (e.g. software engineering).By selecting for unsaturated benchmarks, we risk understating benchmark coverage on O*NET tasks which are easier for LLMs to complete. On the other hand, including saturated benchmarks would risk overstating benchmark coverage if saturation is downstream of lower task realism. The latter claim seems likely, given that benchmarks often overstate LLM performance in real-world deployments. We think that the bias from including saturated benchmarks would be greater than the bias from excluding them, but neither option is ideal.Finally, while we outline our benchmark selection criteria in the Benchmark Index tab, several criteria (like “Economic Realism”) are difficult to formalize and introduce some subjectivity in our choices.Patterns in coverageThe benchmarks in our index have relatively deep and narrow coverage of the overall economy. They disproportionately focus on the economic tasks most exposed to AI automation (as measured by Eloundou et al.), with O*NET tasks rated as “exposed” about 6x more likely to be represented on benchmarks than tasks rated “unexposed”. This makes sense: benchmarks are designed to measure AI progress, and AI progress is most plausible on the most AI-exposed tasks. This explains why benchmarks are full of tasks in Software Engineering and Financial Analysis while sparse on tasks in Truck Driving and Gas Plant Operation.But even after controlling for AI-exposure, O*NET tasks from occupations with larger wage bills are significantly overrepresented among benchmark prompts:Benchmark coverage of O*NET tasks by occupation wage billAdjusted probability of task coverageAnnualized occupation wage bill (log scale)Each point shows the estimated probability that an O*NET task with a given AI-exposure tag belonging to an occupation with a given wage-bill will be covered by at least 5 prompts in our benchmark index. AI-exposure tags are binary and come from Eloundou et al. (2023). Occupation wage-bills are calculated from BLS estimates of the mean wage and number of Americans working in each occupation, assuming a 40 hour work week. Estimated coverage probabilities come from a task-level logistic regression of coverage probability on AI-exposure and log occupational wage bill. Error bars are pointwise 95% delta-method confidence intervals based on standard errors clustered at the occupation group level.After controlling for occupation and AI-exposure score, O*NET “task importance” is another predictor of benchmark coverage. In particular, O*NET tasks come with domain expert estimates of the importance of the task for its occupation on a scale of 1-5. We find that the tasks scored most important are about 6–10x more likely to be represented on benchmarks than those scored least important:Benchmark coverage by O*NET task importance within occupationsAdjusted probability of task coverageO*NET task importance (1–5 rating scale)Each point shows the estimated probability that, controlling for occupation, an O*NET task with a given AI-exposure tag and a given quintile O*NET importance score is covered by at least 5 prompts in our benchmark index. AI-exposure tags are binary and come from Eloundou et al. (2023). Importance quintiles are calculated from O*NET importance scores. Estimated coverage probabilities come from a task-level logistic regression of coverage probability on AI-exposure and importance quintiles, with occupation fixed effects. Error bars are pointwise 95% delta-method confidence intervals based on standard errors clustered at the occupation group level.The plots above suggest a reasonable allocation of the relatively limited resources devoted to high-quality, economically relevant benchmarks so far; it’s natural to prioritize making benchmarks which cover the most important and AI-exposed tasks in the occupations with the largest wage bills. But barring a significant increase in the number and diversity of such benchmarks, these patterns will result in significant blind spots in our view of economically valuable model capabilities.Can O*NET + benchmarks tell us how good AI is at your job?Measuring model capabilities by job occupation is essential – for enterprises deciding which models fit their needs, for policymakers forecasting the economic impact of AI, and for Americans thinking about their careers. Unfortunately, this is a hard problem to solve.We could just try averaging model performance on all benchmark prompts relevant to a given job. But as our Benchmark Map suggests, benchmarks cover some economic tasks much more intensively than others. A simple average would give too much weight to frequently benchmarked tasks.O*NET offers a way to potentially reduce this bias. If we average model performance on occupation-relevant benchmark prompts weighted by O*NET classification, so that each O*NET task is equally weighted in our occupation average, we get a step closer to a number that represents real economic performance.As a first step, we try this approach on Mercor’s APEX benchmarks for four occupations: investment banking, law, accounting, and software engineering. We compare O*NET-weighted scores to simple averages of model performance on tasks related to each occupation. The resulting weighted and unweighted scores are generally quite similar:APEX-1 + APEX-Agents · O*NET: Financial and Investment Analysts · 11 tasks · 176 promptsScore (%)Every prompt counts equallyEvery O*NET task counts equallyClaude Fable 5.1 Max69.8%68.5%Claude Opus 5.5 Max73.3%70.2%Claude Opus 5 Max65.5%63.0%GPT-6 Astra Max65.5%61.8%GPT-5.6 Sol Max66.8%65.6%Grok 4.7 xHigh58.1%58.7%Gemini 3.8 Flash High66.9%67.5%Kimi K3 Max59.4%59.9%DeepSeek V4.1 Flash Max56.5%58.4%For each occupation, we take all prompts across APEX benchmarks related to that occupation. Darker bars show a simple average of model scores on those prompts for each occupation. Then, we sort the prompts by O*NET task. For each O*NET task with at least 5 corresponding APEX prompts, we average model scores on those prompts to get a task-level score. Next, we average each task-level model score to get occupation-level scores which weight performance on each O*NET task equally. (If an O*NET task has fewer than 5 prompts, we drop it from the average). Lighter bars show these weighted scores for each occupation.In this case, at least, O*NET weighting changes very little. Model performance on APEX prompts is similar across the O*NET tasks included in the weighted scores above, which limits the value of reweighting. However, less than ⅓ of the O*NET tasks relevant to the 4 occupations above have enough APEX coverage to be included in our weighted scores. We are hopeful that applying O*NET weighting to a much larger set of benchmarks will result in high-quality occupation-specific model scores, and are working toward that goal.However, even if we incorporate tasks from dozens of benchmarks, several obstacles remain:01How do we navigate low statistical power?The sheer breadth of work done in the US economy means that for any O*NET occupation and task, we have relatively few benchmark items. This means that our estimates are inherently underpowered, and just one or two low-quality items can severely bias our scores.02How do we account for the varying difficulty and fidelity of tasks?Some benchmark items are highly saturated, whereas others are still unsolved. This is partly a function of time (as older benchmarks were designed for less performant models and simpler environments) and partly a function of quality (some benchmark items are simplistically graded, have minor mistakes, or can be reward hacked). We do not yet have an explicit way of weighting by quality.03Can evals that primarily measure AI automation generalize to augmentation?In the real world, AI models are still primarily used by humans, rather than automating entire job functions end-to-end. Therefore, measuring the real-world occupation capabilities of a model should ideally include measuring how much the model augments human productivity. We have completed some early work in this direction, but finding a methodology that scales remains elusive.04Can every O*NET occupation and task be measured with benchmarks?Knowledge-based work is well-suited to measurement through benchmarks because it is largely done on digital machines, like laptops and phones. Dingel and Neiman estimate that only 37% of US jobs could feasibly be done entirely from home, suggesting that ~63% of jobs involve some tasks with a physical-world component which would be hard to incorporate into current benchmarks. For now, this may not be a meaningful oversight – with the rapid development of robotics capabilities, we anticipate a significant need for physical task benchmarks.We are actively working on these problems; if you are too, please reach out!We are indebted to Wang et al. for the O*NET tagging methodology, and thank Nathan Lambert for feedback on a draft of this work.APEX NEWSLETTERThe latest on frontier AI performance, straight to your inbox.New benchmarks, leaderboard shifts, and research from the APEX team.

comments.author: b800h
comments.textZhHtml: 也许是门卫谬误的一个版本，即。用自动门取代门卫似乎是一个明显的胜利，但事实证明门卫正在执行许多其他未被考虑的重要功能（例如客户体验）。

comments.author: etempleton
comments.textZhHtml:
这一直是我在过去几周的论点，以解释为什么我们作为消费者没有看到或感受到现实世界的生产力提高，尽管许多人拥护他们亲眼所见的人工智能在自己的工作流程中的效率。动手工作很少是真正的瓶颈。

我的团队可以在几个小时内完成高质量的工作，人工智能可以在一两分钟内完成相同的中等到高质量的工作，但审查、反馈和签署需要几天的时间来回。人工智能只是减慢了这部分过程，因为编辑人工智能工作通常是一项挑战，因为没有人非常熟悉它是如何组合在一起的，有时它会创建根本无法编辑的东西。告诉人工智能做出非常具体的改变往往是一个好坏参半的问题。

独立开发者和监督最少的小团队可能会移动得更快，但除了无人关注的领域之外，企业将看到最小的提升。

comments.author: majormajor
comments.textZhHtml:
对于成熟的成功公司来说，行动和变革往往比保持静止会带来更直接的风险。在这些公司中，人工智能不一定会带来很多“提高生产力”的收益，因为编写代码并不是瓶颈。但他们中的许多人会试图通过裁员或放慢招聘速度来节省成本。

有几种类型的公司情况恰恰相反：年轻的公司试图发展，而垂死的公司需要扭亏为盈。

在这两种公司中，年轻的公司不太可能按自己的方式行事。因此，你第一个真正看到 AI 带来的更快发展的结果可能是在未来的几个月和几年里，那时大公司突然开始以十年前没有意义的产品和业务策略而广为人知，因为编写代码来尝试不同的事情甚至让事情滚动是一个瓶颈，你只能做一些无法长期扩展的事情。

comments.author: dingdongditchme
comments.textZhHtml: 或者说，生产力的提高虽然很大，但并不像法学硕士提供商让您相信的那样是惊天动地的。与任何新技术一样，采用都是落后的。互联网“存在”于20世纪80年代末90年代初。许多公司仍然通过首先介入这一领域来获得生产力的提高。

我从事代码生成工作，经常感到这样的谬论：“因为我可以在一天内构建出与您的产品看起来 80% 相似的东西，您应该付给我 N 百万美元。”

这与 15 年前的 Ruby on Rails 人群和 5 年前的无代码人群的宣传大致相同。

很少有公司需要每周重建他们的产品，或者真正关心什么技术堆栈它继续运行。他们正在尝试构建新的事物，或者减少这些事物损坏的频率，或者弄清楚下一步是否值得构建什么。

comments.author: thelastgallon
comments.textZhHtml:
> 单独的开发人员和监督最少的小团队可能会进展得更快

完全正确！

通常，团队中的大多数工作都会因执行决策而减慢。需要 3 - 9 个月的时间才能对某件事做出是/否的决定，对于大多数明显需要完成的事情，都需要向上级指挥。决策需要很长时间，但当决策做出后，他们希望事情能够快速完成，这对 IC 造成了不合理的压力。

看到真正生产力提升的第一步是人工智能消除执行层和中层管理层，这会启动一个良性循环，破坏帝国建设并大幅加速真正的生产力，而不仅仅是像 LOC 这样毫无意义的指标。

说实话，你在这里走错了方向。短期内最有可能的情况是，管理层将寻求用由骨干人员支持的自动化系统取代劳动力，以帮助实施和执行级别的任务，这些任务不能（或不应该）由法学硕士单独处理，例如部署。

stories.title: Solar surpasses nuclear power globally for first time
stories.titleZh: Solar surpasses nuclear power globally for first time
stories.author: xbmcuser
summaryZh: Solar and wind are increasingly outpacing nuclear power globally, with solar generation surpassing nuclear for the first time in 2025, according to WNISR 2026. The report highlights nuclear’s slow growth, lengthy construction timelines and limited small modular reactor deployment, contrasting them with rapid renewables and battery expansion. The World Nuclear Industry Status Report (WNISR) 2026, overseen by French nuclear energy consultant Mycle Schneider, shows that wind power alone surpassed nuclear generation on a monthly basis in March 2025, followed by solar in April – the first time global monthly solar generation exceeded nuclear output.

From March 2025 through June 2026, either solar or wind individually generated more electricity than nuclear every month. In March, April and May 2026, both technologies independently surpassed nuclear generation.

comments.author: philipkglass
comments.textZhHtml:
Note that this is actual generated terawatt hours. Nuclear power has a substantially higher capacity factor, but solar has been growing so rapidly that it has taken the lead on generated output too. Wind is just about to surpass nuclear generation also, though solar is racing ahead much faster. The next big milestone, not to be reached for several years at the present rate, would be solar generation overtaking hydroelectric generation. You can see data up through 2025 here:

https://ourworldindata.org/electricity-mix

Even though solar power has been a significant part of the energy conversation for decades, the majority of solar growth is very recent. Nuclear power generated 2762 TWh in 2021, when solar generated 1054 TWh. Solar power generated 2779 TWh in 2025.

comments.author: silvestrov
comments.textZhHtml:
An interesting fact is that China has passed "peak coal" in 2024 while still growing with about 5% in a year.

Denmark had peak coal early (2003) due to early investments in wind power. Coal is now practically gone.

We might see China get the same shift in electricity source as Denmark had over the past 20 years, just much faster.

comments.author: jakobnissen

stories.title: The Elizabeth Holmes documentary “You Can See Everything” is deceiving
stories.titleZh: The Elizabeth Holmes documentary “You Can See Everything” is deceiving
stories.author: MaysonL
summaryZh: Holy freaking cow.I saw the new Elizabeth Holmes documentary, You Can See Everything, last night, and I genuinely can’t type fast enough to express how mind-bending it was.I’ve seen a lot of chatter online about whether Elizabeth Holmes is a liar, whether she deserves to be in prison for her failed startup Theranos, and whether the documentary is too sympathetic to her.But that’s not even remotely close to what I took away from it. As we walked out, my husband asked me, “So what did you think?” And I just responded with, “Forget Elizabeth Holmes. That was a masterpiece in storytelling.”Enjoying this? I write The Profile — original longform profiles of extraordinary people, free every week since 2017. Join the club:I walked in expecting that the filmmakers were going to tell us a story about deception. What I did not expect is that they were deceiving us — the viewers — in real time. An entire theater full of grown adults was falling for it. At one point, people were shouting so loudly at the screen that I couldn’t hear the dialogue. I heard a woman yell, “Criminal!” — and it wasn’t directed at Elizabeth Holmes. I’ve never experienced anything like that in a movie theater. It was emotion, and it was visceral.What makes the documentary so brilliant is that it forces you to confront how much of what you believe about another person comes how their story has been told to you. And we are so so susceptible to this that it’s scary.Think about Elizabeth Holmes. How much of your opinion of her comes from the facts of her criminal case & how much comes from the images and/or videos and/or TV dramas you’ve seen over the years? I remember one Halloween when the Theranos scandal was at its peak, it seemed like everyone was dressed in a black turtleneck carrying tiny vials of fake blood. Holmes was everywhere.But the thing that often gets lost in the retelling of her story is that Holmes was actually acquitted of all four charges related to defrauding patients. She’s in prison because a jury found that she knowingly misled investors who poured more than $700 million into the startup. That’s a significant distinction, but as a society, we don’t love nuance. Just tell us — is she good or is she bad? Is she a liar or is she not?I recently wrote about a fascinating experiment Canon conducted in 2015. Six photographers were asked to photograph the same man in the same location. The twist was that each photographer was given a different description of him: a millionaire, a convict, a fisherman, an alcoholic, a psychic, and a lifesaver.The resulting portraits were wildly different.A Canon rep said, “A photograph is shaped more by the person behind the camera than by what’s in front of it.”Now imagine that principle applied to an entire three-hour documentary.Over the course of the film, directors Lance Oppenheim and Nathan Fielder managed to make a theater full of people with fully developed pre-frontal cortexes repeatedly reconsider what they believed about the people on screen. They did it through camera angles, close-ups, editing, and the order in which information was revealed. The framing of Elizabeth and those around her changed little by little until it became obvious, and as soon as our brains detected a narrative shift, our feelings about it followed. It was like watching a magic show … or one continuous reality TV show in which someone gets the villain edit, the victim edit, the manipulator edit, and all of us just falling for it again and again.If this kind of storytelling breakdown is your thing, you’ll love The Profile. I explore how powerful people are framed — and how they frame themselves — every week. Subscribe for free:We like to believe that we form our opinions by gathering evidence, weighing facts, and arriving at reasonable conclusions. Be for real. No we do not. Here’s how it actually goes: We form an emotional impression first, then we build a belief around it, and then we go looking for facts that support it. This is my theory as to why we’re so divided in this country. Beliefs built on emotion are nearly impossible to reason with. The psychology behind the film’s manipulation should be studied. First, a close-up shot of an unblinking Elizabeth Holmes: She’s sinister. Then, a wider shot of her bouncing her baby: Wait a second, she’s a mom, she’s human! Then, her husband’s painstakingly long pause: Wait, is he the puppeteer? Then, a smile! “No, no, that can’t be genuine.”And then there’s Fielder himself, who moved in with the couple for a whole month before Holmes headed to prison. How reliable of a narrator is he? Does he care a bit too much for Elizabeth that he’s willing to lie to the viewer? How much can we trust his perception of events?I’m telling you, it’'ll break your brain.You Can See Everything does a good job explaining the phenomenon of psychological manipulation, but it also makes you participate in it. It evokes emotion, and all of the greatest pieces of art evoke emotion. You sit there believing you’re watching a documentary about a woman who deceived the world, only to discover that you’re also watching a demonstration of how easy it is to deceive you.(This was really hard to write without giving away any spoilers, but watch the film, and let me know what you think!)

comments.textZhHtml:
Nathan Fielder is pretty well-known for his work in The Rehearsal and Nathan for You. Nathan for You resides in the docu-comedy genre, where you take advantage of real people's reactions to absurd situations for comedic effect. Other examples are things like Kitchen Nightmares (where Gordon Ramsey goes into real restaurants and "fixes" them). It's a well-done version of the idea, but not revolutionary IMO.

The Rehearsal, however, extends the idea further. In that show, he helps real people "rehearse" for hard conversations. It involves Fielder building extravagant sets and having absurdly detailed set-ups with multiple actors, then running the conversation multiple times. What makes this "different" is that now the real person is partially in on it? Like, they know that they're on a set. They know that this is a simulation. So the show is more "meta" than previous entries in the genre, opening up other avenues for humour.

I say this because You Can See Everything is best understood as a further extension of those projects. Even the name indicates this, because by nature of a documentary, you can't see everything. You have a real person in Elizabeth Holmes, being interviewed by a person in Fielder that's known for his stunts taking advantage of "real people," where he watches fictionalized versions of Holmes with Holmes herself? Viewed in light of his previous projects, this feels like an extension of them.

But even with that, I think the setup does allow you to see something real in Holmes. She also knows how people "want" to see her! So there's also a sort of meta-narrative there too, where you know Holmes is on her best behavior to try and dispel the narrative from those fictionalized TV characterizations. The fact that she comes off poorly in the documentary says something, even accounting for the fact that Fielder is trying to sell a narrative.

It's a real mind game, but I think it's representative of Holmes because of that. She is going to jail for a fraud that amounts to a similar sort of mind game, she agrees to a documentary to show herself differently, but that documentary is also a mind game. Wild stuff.

summaryZh: We've said before that Claude writes about 90 percent of Claude Code's own code. So how do we review code at the volume we produce it? Does anyone read code anymore? And if something breaks, who catches it? This post covers the code review flow on the Claude Code team and how it has evolved. From June to September, merged pull requests to Claude Code's codebase more than doubled while the share that had to be reverted fell by more than 40 percent. We didn't remove review. But we did move most of the reading to machines, optimized for human time and attention, and invested heavily in making it fast and easy to undo mistakes. RETHINKING THE PURPOSE OF CODE REVIEW When agents write code, the number of changes goes up, fast. In Anthropic's monorepo, changes landing per day went from about 2,500 in May to more than 30,000 in September this year. Claude Code lives in its own repository, separate from the monorepo, but it's seeing a lot of pressure too. When you are shipping this fast, manual, line-by-line code review is incredibly difficult if not impossible. Code review does two jobs:
Find and fix issues before they ship Build shared context and codebase understanding across the team

它还混合了重要和不重要的信息。它倾向于认为提交/错误修复很重要，并且很乐意将其与功能的重要属性一起列出。

至少 Opus 5.5 做到了这一点。不过，它的写作比其他模型要好。我让其他模型用难以理解的语言解释了一些东西，技术上是正确的，但实际上并不是什么内容。

comments.author: elondaits
comments.textZhHtml: I hate it when it realizes something that was contextually obvious to me, and then treats it like a precious nugget of wisdom, including it in the README, the comments, and the commit message. Even worse when it’s a hypothetical situation. “Even if the raw chicken is bagged and refrigerated, we want to avoid a leaky bag.”

comments.author: bulbar
comments.textZhHtml:
I believe this is a variant of it: I dislike how often it mentions stuff that's not there or relevant (anymore), just because it was referenced somewhere:
"We use a double instead of a float there so that the addition will not overflow". Yeah, thanks, that was a bug 2 years ago, nobody cares that the line now does what it's supposed to do.

comments.author: IshKebab
comments.textZhHtml:
They pretty much fixed that. Plus you can influence the writing style to some extent. I tell it to use full sentences and avoid assuming I already understand the code.

Another thing is that it's very good at creating diagrams (I think someone wrote a skill for it so maybe not by default). I usually find the diagrams are even more valuable than the text.

Honestly I was skeptical but you really can just point Claude at some code and ask it to make a markdown + SVG explainer and it will do a shockingly good job.

I'd still rather read human documentation, but even before AI almost nobody writes any - especially for internal code. And they certainly don't make great diagrams.
